title: Price marking and overcharging
act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
summary: Traders must display prices for goods and may not sell above the marked or controlled price.
keyPoints: Prices must be clearly displayed
Selling above the marked price is an offence
Complaints can be made to the Consumer Affairs Authority
penalty: Fines and, in some cases, imprisonment under the Act. Verify current amounts.
example: A shop charges Rs. 50 above the printed price on a packet. You can complain to the CAA hotline 1977.

title: Rights over defective goods
act: Consumer Affairs Authority Act No. 9 of 2003
summary: Consumers can seek a remedy when goods or services are defective or not as described.
keyPoints: Keep your receipt as proof
Ask for a repair, replacement or refund
Escalate to the CAA if the seller refuses
penalty: Remedies depend on the case: refund, replacement, or CAA action against the trader.
example: A phone stops working in two days. Show the receipt and request a replacement or refund.

title: Carrying a valid driving licence
summary: A driver must hold a valid licence for the class of vehicle and produce it when asked by police.
keyPoints: Licence must match the vehicle class
Carry the licence and vehicle documents
Expired or missing licences can lead to fines
penalty: Fine on conviction or on-the-spot fine procedure. Verify current amounts.
example: A police officer stops you at a checkpoint and asks for your licence. You must present it.

title: Drink driving
summary: Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs is a serious offence.
keyPoints: Police may test drivers
Licence can be suspended
Applies to all vehicle types
penalty: Fine, imprisonment, and possible licence suspension or disqualification.
example: A driver is tested after a minor collision and found over the limit. He can be charged in court.

title: EPF and ETF contributions
act: Employees' Provident Fund Act No. 15 of 1958 and Employees' Trust Fund Act No. 46 of 1980
summary: Employers must contribute to the EPF and ETF for eligible employees.
keyPoints: Employer contributes 12% to EPF and employee 8%
Employer contributes 3% to ETF
You can check your balance with the Central Bank / ETF Board
penalty: Employers who fail to pay can face surcharges and legal action by the Labour Department.
example: Your employer deducts EPF from your salary but does not remit it. You can complain to the Labour Department.

title: Maternity leave
summary: Women employees are entitled to paid maternity leave.
keyPoints: 84 working days for the first two living children
Shorter period for later children
Employer must not dismiss for pregnancy
penalty: Employers who breach it can be prosecuted. Verify details for your sector.
example: A private-sector employee is denied leave for her second child. She can report to the Labour Department.

title: Transfer of land requires a notarial deed
act: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
summary: A sale or transfer of land must be in writing and executed before a Notary Public and witnesses.
keyPoints: Verbal agreements are not enough
Register the deed at the Land Registry
Check the title before buying
penalty: An improperly executed transfer may be invalid and unenforceable.
example: A buyer pays for land on a handwritten note only. The transfer is at risk of being void without a notarial deed.

title: Ownership by long possession
summary: Uninterrupted and adverse possession of immovable property for ten years can give rights of ownership.
keyPoints: Possession must be continuous and without the owner's consent
Applies to immovable property
A court must usually declare the title
penalty: No penalty. The remedy is a court declaration of title.
example: A family farms a plot openly for over ten years while the owner never objects. They may claim title by prescription.

title: Unauthorized access to computers
summary: Accessing a computer or account without authority is a criminal offence.
keyPoints: Hacking and password theft are covered
Spreading data obtained illegally is an offence
Report to the police or SL CERT
penalty: Fine and imprisonment depending on the offence.
example: A student logs into a friend's social media account without permission and posts messages. This may be an offence.

title: Personal data rights
act: Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022
summary: Individuals have rights over how organizations collect and use their personal data.
keyPoints: Right to access your data
Right to correct inaccurate data
Organizations must process data lawfully
penalty: Penalties are imposed by the Data Protection Authority. Check implementation status.
example: A company collects your details for one purpose and sells them. You can complain to the authority.

title: Maintenance for spouse and children
summary: Parents and spouses may be required to provide financial maintenance, claimed in the Magistrate's Court.
keyPoints: Children are entitled to maintenance
Application is made to the Magistrate's Court
Court sets the amount based on needs and means
penalty: Non-payment of a court order can lead to enforcement and imprisonment.
example: A father stops supporting his child after separation. The mother can apply for a maintenance order.

title: Protection from domestic violence
act: Prevention of Domestic Violence Act No. 34 of 2005
summary: Victims of domestic violence can apply for a protection order from the Magistrate's Court.
keyPoints: Covers physical and emotional harm
Protection orders can bar the abuser from the home
Police can assist in urgent situations
penalty: Breach of a protection order is an offence leading to fine or imprisonment.
example: A woman is repeatedly threatened at home. She can approach the police or court for a protection order.

title: Right to Information
act: Right to Information Act No. 12 of 2016
summary: Citizens can request information held by public authorities.
keyPoints: Submit a written request to the Information Officer
A response is due within 14 working days
Appeal to the RTI Commission if refused
penalty: Officers who refuse without a valid reason may face penalties.
example: You request details of a public school's fund use. The authority must respond or give a lawful reason.
